query: I am investigating a quaternary equiatomic alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure, specifically looking for the relationship between its mechanical properties and its corrosion resistance. What hypotheses can be proposed regarding the plastic deformation mechanisms under uniaxial tension? Please provide supporting prior evidence for dislocation-based yielding, identify the boundary conditions where yield strength might become insensitive to strain rate, and propose a falsification experiment to distinguish between dislocation glide and phase transformation mechanisms.

generation.target_system: Quaternary equiatomic High Entropy Alloy (HEA) with Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) structure, investigated under uniaxial tension at ambient to moderate temperatures to assess plastic deformation mechanisms and their correlation with corrosion resistance.

evidence_appraisal.record_system: Quinary Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (Refractory HEA), processed via HIP and annealing, resulting in mixed HCP/FCC phases.
evidence_appraisal.difference_from_target: Target is quaternary and single-phase FCC; this record is quinary, contains HCP phases, and exhibits brittle fracture under tension. The processing (HIP) induced HCP, unlike the target's assumed stable FCC.
evidence_appraisal.reason: Different crystal structure (HCP presence) and failure mode (brittle vs. ductile) make the deformation mechanism (brittle fracture) inapplicable to the target's FCC ductile regime.

generation.hypothesis: In the quaternary equiatomic FCC HEA, plastic deformation under uniaxial tension will be governed by dislocation glide on {111} planes and the formation of deformation twins and stacking faults, similar to the Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi). The yield strength will be dominated by solid solution strengthening due to severe lattice distortion. At low strain rates and moderate temperatures, the yield strength will become insensitive to strain rate due to the dominance of thermally activated cross-slip and the high stacking fault energy (or low, depending on specific elements) facilitating twin nucleation rather than dislocation climb. The boundary condition for strain-rate insensitivity is expected when the thermal activation energy for dislocation motion is sufficient to overcome lattice friction, typically at temperatures >0.3 Tm (where Tm is melting point) or at very low strain rates where diffusion-assisted processes (though less likely in FCC at RT) or cross-slip dominate.
generation.material_initial_state: Quaternary equiatomic HEA (e.g., CoCrFeMn, CoCrNiFe, or similar) in a single-phase Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) solid solution state, likely annealed to remove processing defects but retaining high dislocation density from synthesis.
generation.intervention: Uniaxial tensile testing at varying strain rates (e.g., 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-1 s^-1) and temperatures (e.g., 77 K to 600 K) to probe the transition between dislocation glide and phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tension, strain rates: 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1, Temperatures: 77 K to 600 K, Environment: Inert or air (to correlate with corrosion resistance if tested in situ, though mechanical test is primary).
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation networks, stacking faults, and deformation twins (nano-twins) within the FCC lattice. Potential transient HCP phase formation at twin boundaries or high-stress regions.
generation.mechanism: Based on the transfer of evidence from PMC7229066 and PMC6093928, the mechanism is dislocation glide on {111} planes coupled with the nucleation and growth of deformation twins and stacking faults. The high configurational entropy leads to severe lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation motion (solid solution strengthening) but promotes twinning as a secondary deformation mode to accommodate strain. The transition from dislocation glide to phase transformation (FCC to HCP) is hypothesized to occur at cryogenic temperatures or high strain rates where the stacking fault energy is effectively lowered by the stress state, similar to the Cantor alloy behavior described in PMC6093928.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy will exhibit high yield strength and significant ductility. The stress-strain curve will show a continuous hardening regime. At low temperatures (77 K), a significant contribution from deformation twinning will be observed, potentially leading to an FCC-to-HCP transformation at twin boundaries. At higher temperatures (>300 K) and low strain rates, the yield strength will plateau (become insensitive to strain rate) as cross-slip becomes the rate-limiting step. The correlation with corrosion resistance will likely show that the high dislocation density and twin boundaries act as preferential sites for corrosion initiation, reducing overall resistance compared to a defect-free single crystal.
generation.baseline: Conventional FCC alloys (e.g., pure Ni or Cu) where deformation is dominated by dislocation glide with minimal twinning, and yield strength is less sensitive to strain rate at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for single-phase FCC equiatomic HEAs. It fails if the alloy decomposes into intermetallics or BCC phases (as seen in PMC5578249 or PMC5978046) or if the stacking fault energy is so high that twinning is suppressed entirely.
generation.uncertainty: The exact strain rate and temperature threshold for the transition to strain-rate insensitivity is uncertain due to the specific composition of the quaternary alloy (which affects stacking fault energy). The extent of the FCC-to-HCP transformation is also uncertain and depends on the specific elements chosen.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) during uniaxial tension at cryogenic temperatures (77 K) and room temperature. Compare the evolution of diffraction peaks and microstructure at two distinct strain rates (10^-4 s^-1 and 10^-1 s^-1).
measurements: Appearance of HCP (100) or (101) peaks (phase transformation)
Dislocation density and twin spacing via TEM
Stress-strain curve slope (strain hardening rate) vs. strain rate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hypothesis is correct, a distinct FCC-to-HCP phase transformation should be observed via XRD at 77 K, and the yield strength should show a strong dependence on strain rate at 77 K but become insensitive at room temperature. If the yield strength remains highly sensitive to strain rate at room temperature, or if no HCP phase is detected at cryogenic temperatures despite high stress, the hypothesis regarding the dominance of twinning/phase transformation over pure dislocation glide is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper examines the microstructure and mechanical properties of Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 . Two casting processes, namely, gravity casting and suction-assisted casting, were applied, both followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). The aim of the current study was to investigate the creep and tensile properties of the material, since the literature review revealed no data whatsoever regarding these properties. The main findings are that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings. The HIP process also led to a considerable increase in the mechanical properties of both materials under compression, with values found to be higher than those reported in the literature. Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C. Fractography yielded brittle fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation prior to fracture.

Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. Nanomaterials are new age materials exhibiting exceptional mechanical, electronic, and optical properties due to their unique structure and high surface-area to volume ratio [ [1] ]. Among nanomaterials, one dimensional (1D) metallic nanowires (NWs) are widely used for different applications including nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, energy harvesting and storage, ultrasensitive sensing, and nanoelectromechanical devices [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. At the nanoscale, 1D NWs usually exhibit ultra high strength, differently from bulk materials, which makes them ideal candidates for studying their fundamental deformation mechanisms. Dislocation nucleation from free surfaces and its subsequent propagation through NWs has been found to be a dominant deformation mechanism in metallic NWs such as Au, Ag, Cu, and Ni [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This enables reorientation to a more preferred phase, resulting in exceptional mechanical properties such as superplasticity, high yielding strength, pseudoelasticity, and shape memory effects [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ].
